Items.Authors: Coby Silayan, Suresh Sivanandam, Aaron Tohuvavohu, Albert Lau, Mark Barnet, Patrick Nkwari, Shaojie Chen, Gavin Hay, Jean Christophe Fronteddu, Norbert Werner, András Pál, Marianna Dafčíková, Emily Hu, Filip Munz, Jakub Ripa, Andy Gong
Items.Title: A report on the First Technology Demonstration mission of the Little UV Camera (LUVCam1)
Items.Abstract: Here we report on the status of the first on-orbit technology demonstration of the Little UV Camera (LUVCam1). LUVCam1 is a 0.4U payload aboard the 2U cubesat GRBBeta that was launched in July 2024. The primary objective of the mission was to qualify the GSENSE4040 CMOS sensor and its readout electronics in preparation for the Quick UltraVIolet Kilonova Surveyor (QUVIK; Werner et al. 2023) satellite. LUVCam will serve as the primary scientific camera for this mission. We report on the performance of the GSENSE4040-FSI sensor used on LUVCam1, beginning with its in-lab characterization followed by an assessment of its on-orbit performance using astronomical observations made by LUVCam1. The camera remains operational two years later and has taken pictures of coastlines, the moon, and stars that we show here. Through LUVCam1, we demonstrated an approach leveraging new-space to qualify the latest COTS CMOS sensors for astronomy missions.

Items.Authors: Gaurav Waratkar, Hiromasa Miyasaka, Brian W. Grefenstette, Fiona A. Harrison
Items.Title: Beyond NuSTAR: Characterization of thicker, broadband Redlen CdZnTe detectors for next-generation X-ray telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) advanced hard X-ray imaging with its CZT pixel detectors, but with limited count rate capability and spectral bandwidth. Future hard X-ray telescopes need better spectral resolution, higher throughput, and improved quantum efficiency across a wider band, along with smaller pixels to complement modern optics. We present the development and characterization of new Redlen CZT detectors that are 2 cm × 2 cm in area and 3 mm thick, making them 50 percent thicker than NuSTAR’s detectors. Using NuSTAR heritage ASIC, we measure key detector properties including leakage current, inter-pixel conductance, gain uniformity, and depth of interaction performance. Our results show that these thicker CZT detectors deliver higher quantum efficiency and stable spectral response across a broader energy range, establishing a strong path forward for future hard X-ray missions in the NASA Explorer and Probe classes.

Items.Authors: Naoyuki Tamura, Yuki Moritani, Kiyoto Yabe, Shintaro Koshida, Masahiro Takada, Hitoshi Murayama, Masayuki Tanaka, Yukiko Kamata, Akira Arai, Miho N. Ishigaki, Wanqiu He, Sogo Mineo, Takahiro Morishima, Michitaro Koike, Makoto Tanaka, Matthew Wung, Kumiko Morihana, Sadman Ali, Takashi Hattori, Tae-Soo Pyo, Zhuoming Li, Wilfred T. Gee, Vera M. Passegger, James E. Gunn, Robert H. Lupton, Craig P. Loomis, Arnaud Le Fur, Paul Price, Michael A. Strauss, Shiang-Yu Wang, Chi-Hung Yan, Jennifer L. Karr, Stephen A. Smee, Randolph P. Hammond, Joshua Peebles, Timothy M. Heckman, Jared Siegel, Christian K. Jespersen
Items.Title: ʻŌnohiʻula - Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS) for the Subaru telescope: progresses and challenges towards and following the Science First Light
Items.Abstract: Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS) for the Subaru Telescope, which was recently given the Hawaiian name “ʻŌnohiʻula”, is now in the first year of its science operation. This instrument is an extremely wide-field (1.3 degree in diameter), fiber-fed multi-object (2,386 operating fibers), optical & near-infrared spectrometer (380-1260nm). All hardware components were installed on the Subaru Telescope in August 2024. While on-sky engineering tests and performance verifications have been continuously carried out since the fall of 2021 in parallel to hardware and software integration, the science operation began in the first semester of 2025 (S25A) with the first program from March 22 (i.e., Science First Light). We will report the progress of this instrument with resolved and continuing challenges.

Items.Authors: Fernando Rueda-Teruel, Axel Yanes-Díaz, Sergio Rueda-Teruel, Rafael Bello, Jorge Ventura-Guillamón, Mikel Domínguez-Martínez, Nuria Martínez-Olivar, Juan Manuel Olivas-Galve, Guillermo López-Alegre, Sergio Chueca, Luis Alberto Rodríguez-García, Raúl Domínguez, Héctor de Paz, Manuel Huertas, César Iñiguez, Antonio Marín-Franch, Tamara Civera, José Javier Collado-Escusa, María Rosario Mayoral-Blasco, Jordi Albero-Gamir, David Garcés-Cubel, Said Farah-Amin, María Almarcegui-Gracia, A. Javier Cenarro, Romano Corradi, Mariano Moles, Carlos López-Sanjuan, Héctor Vázquez-Ramió, Javier Zaragoza-Cardiel, Luisa Valdivielso-Casas, Javier Lizaga-Villarroya, Stelios Pyrzas, Miguel Chioare Díaz-Martín, Ramón Iglesias-Marzoa, Clara Cabanillas-de-la-Casa, Natalio Maícas-Sacristán, José Luis Lamadrid-Gutiérrez, Fátima López-Martínez, Francisco José Galindo-Guil, Elvis Lacruz-Calderón, Juan Castillo, Ángel López-Sainz, Mohammad Akhlaghi, Javier Hernández-Fuertes, David José Muniesa-Gallardo, Alberto Moreno-Signes, Antonio Hernán-Caballero, Giacomo Lorenzetti, Alessandro Ederoclite, Juan Antonio Fernández-Ontiveros, Raúl Infante-Sainz, Sepideh Eskandarlou, David Fernández-Gil, Adrián Hidalgo-Pinilla, David Morate-González, Nischal Acharya, Borja Anguiano, Karla Ziboney Arellano-Cordova, Sayali Kulkarni, David Martínez-Delgado, Bojan Novakovic, Francisco Javier Sáez-Ruiz, Stefano Zarattini, Silvia Vaquero-Valer, Inés Muñoz-Igado, María Teresa Alegre-Sánchez, Gema María Julián-Caballero-de-España, Rosa Allueva-Gómez, Ana López-Colás
Items.Title: OPTIMIA: an AI-enabled maintenance assistant for critical observatory infrastructure at the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory
Items.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform maintenance in astronomical observatories by moving from corrective and fixed preventive routines towards predictive and condition-based strategies. We present OPTIMIA, an AI-enabled maintenance framework being developed at the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory (OAJ) to support technicians and managers through sensor data, maintenance records and a virtual assistant. OPTIMIA acts as a multi-agent AI layer over the existing Global Observatory Control System, correlating telemetry, SCADA alarms, maintenance data and documented knowledge while leaving deterministic control and safety layers untouched. Initial targets include diesel generators, glycol-water pumps, HVAC plants, electrical distribution and liquid-nitrogen supply. Early prototypes are being deployed in supervised shadow-mode workflows to detect degradation, support intervention-window recommendations and improve documentation, prioritisation and data-driven decisions.

Items.Authors: Paulo H. Silva, William Schoenell, Antonio N. Kanaan
Items.Title: Chimera Observatory Control System
Items.Abstract: Chimera is a Python-based OCS designed to streamline the automation and robotization of astronomical observatories. Addressing the need for flexible and scalable observatory management, Chimera employs a distributed architecture built on network-accessible components. Its object-oriented design organizes observatory devices into two interface types: Instruments and Controllers. Instruments provide unified interfaces for hardware such as mounts, cameras, and focusers, abstracting device-specific controls. Controllers leverage these interfaces to implement higher-level behaviors, including focus modeling, observation scheduling, and safety monitoring.  This presentation details the technical process of modernizing Chimera, highlighting the impact of Python’s evolution on scientific software development. We showcase real-world examples of observatories currently operating legacy versions of Chimera that are transitioning to the updated system, as well as new observatories.

Items.Authors: Ellen Lee, Mark Chun, Ruihan Zhang, Olivier Lai, Michael Connelley, Tony Denault, Jacob Taylor, John Rayner, Max Baeten, Arjo Bos, Matias Kidron, Fred Kamphues, Stefan Kuiper, Wouter Jonker, Alan Ryan, Philip Hinz
Items.Title: Improving the throughput of facility instruments with IRTF-ASM-1
Items.Abstract: The IRTF adaptive secondary mirror (ASM) has been functioning well since first light in April 2024. Although primarily intended as an on-sky demonstration of the new hybrid variable reluctance (HVR) actuator technology, we are working to “facilitize” the ASM for nightly use to improve the sensitivity of facility instruments at the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF). The ASM is operated using the facility wavefront sensor FELIX, which is a 2x2 Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor that uses a frame transfer CCD. We present our current progress in the facility integration of IRTF-ASM-1, including calibration techniques with seeing-limited instruments, software upgrades to streamline the operation of the system, and a demonstration of different observing modes with the ASM.

Items.Authors: Lukas R. Stone, Abraham D. Falcone, Joseph M. Colosimo, Mitchell Wages, Timothy Emeigh, Kadri M. Nizam, Md. Arman Hossen, Laurel ONeill, Ian T. Ashcroft, William A. Bevidas, Brynn Bortree, Zachary E. Catlin, Sierra Deppe, Killian Gremling, Abigail A. Raytsis
Items.Title: A low-noise small-pixel hybrid CMOS detector for future x-ray observatories
Items.Abstract: The Pennsylvania State University High-Energy Astrophysics Detector and Instrumentation Lab, in collaboration with Teledyne Imaging Sensors (TIS), has developed a next-generation small-pixel soft X-ray hybrid CMOS detector (HCD). The Small-Pixel1024 is an HCD with a 1024x1024 grid of 12.5-micron pitch pixels, featuring a high-gain capacitive transimpedance amplifier and in-pixel correlated double sampling. The Small-pixel1024 has full-frame readout speeds of up to 149 frames/s and readout rates in excess of 1 kHz in a windowed mode. Two separate pixel designs were developed using different charge-injection schemes to restore pixel full-well post pixel reset, allowing for X-ray sensitivity up to 20 keV. Here, we report on the methods and results for the characterization and optimization of the Small-Pixel1024 dark current, read noise, gain variation, and energy resolution, including a comparison between the two pixel types.

Items.Authors: Christine Gregg, John C. Mather, Eliad Peretz, Othman Oudghiri-Idrissi, Omar M. Marey, Jamila Taaki, Stuart B. Shaklan, Ahmed Soliman, Rhonda M. Morgan
Items.Title: Hybrid observatory for earthlike exoplanets: concepts for dynamically stable constructed starshades
Items.Abstract: The Hybrid Observatory for Earthlike Exoplanets (HOEE) is a mission concept that envisions imaging Earth-sized exoplanets around exoplanets using an earth-based telescope and orbiting starshade. To meet propulsion requirements, the starshade must meet stringent mass requirements while maintaining high levels of shape precision under station keeping loads during observation. In this paper, we describe robotic assembly concepts for a 100m starshade. We first characterize the anticipated dynamic structural requirements given anticipated station keeping loads required to keep the starshade aligned during an observation. We then analyze several structural designs suitable for robotic assem

Items.Authors: Frank Groark, Peter Thompson, Mauro Manetti, Matteo Tintori, Pierluigi Fumi, Hugo Chiquito, John Spanos, Francesco Leonardi, Daniele Gallieni, Roberto Biasi, Glenn Brossus
Items.Title: GMT ASM status and phasing test results
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope uses a 7 segment adaptive secondary mirror array to correct atmospheric turbulence, wind-induced jitter, and alignment errors. Each 1.05 m off-axis segment has a 2 mm face sheet actuated by 675 magnetically coupled voice-coil motors, and a positioner hexapod maintaining 7 Hz alignment. Diffraction limited performance in NGS and LTAO modes requires phasing of the seven ASM and seven M1 sub-apertures at the image plane. Wavefront based phasing is augmented by edge sensors to maintain vertex alignment during latency, making phasing a key GMT performance risk. Under an NSF risk-reduction program, GMTO and AdOptica developed an ASM Phasing Testbed using one operational segment in a frame simulating three neighbors. Wind disturbances are injected via the hexapod, measured by edge sensors, and corrected through a 2 kHz face sheet control loop. Measured error-budget terms are used to correlate finite-element models, used to refine full-array phasing predictions.

Items.Authors: Johannes G. Staguhn, Dale J. Fixsen, Elmer H. Sharp, Mario D. Cabrera, Daniel P. Kelly, Stephen F. Maher, Avi M. Mandell, Craig W. McMurtry, Gregory Mosby, Peter C. Nagler
Items.Title: A HgCdTe detector-based mid-infrared spectrometer for space-based exoplanet transit and phase curve observations
Items.Abstract: We present a modified HgCdTe detector-based laboratory demonstration of an ultra-stable mid-IR array spectrometer for exoplanet transits. The instrument includes a calibration system that enables the 1/f stability required for the detection of atmospheric bio-signatures in habitable-zone planets around M-dwarfs. We have already demonstrated the required stability of 5 ppm with Transition Edge Sensors (TES) over days in an identical spectrometer. However, TES require sub-K cooling. In 2019 Cabrera et al. demonstrated a long-wavelength cut-off of 16.7 μm for a new HgCdTe-based detector, and Mandell et al., 2022, demonstrated that this long-wavelength cutoff would be sufficient to measure surface temperature, radius, and multiple atmospheric tracers. We use this particular array in our demonstration. Here, we provide an overview of the testbed and present first results from ongoing tests and compare these to the performance we achieved with TES detectors.

Items.Authors: Jun Kajihara, Yuji Ikeda, Koki Isoyama, Hidehito Himeno, Masatsugu Kamiura, Daisuke Yamanaka
Items.Title: FEM-based thermal deformation analysis of large Fine Cordierite mirrors induced by CTE   inhomogeneity
Items.Abstract: Fine Cordierite® is a promising mirror material for large telescopes, offering ultra-low thermal expansion comparable to ULE® or ZERODUR®, with superior stiffness and thermal conductivity. However, spatial inhomogeneity in its coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) can cause surface figure errors when temperature deviates from polishing conditions.  Isoyama et al. (2024) first measured Fine Cordierite's CTE inhomogeneity and characterized it as a structure function, but the impact on large mirrors and mitigation strategies remained unclear.  This study develops a design methodology to predict and suppress CTE inhomogeneity effects. We establish a simulation framework integrating statistically representative spatial CTE distributions into Finite Element Method models to compute thermal deformation and quantify surface figure errors. We then investigate backside rib structure optimization to minimize thermally induced deformation, demonstrating the approach's effectiveness.

Items.Authors: Nikhil More, Kirpal Nandra, Walfried Raab, Hermine Schnetler, Hilda Kinter, Andreas von Kienlin, Sebastian Albrecht, Javier Veredas, Andreas Lederhuber, Astrid Mayr, Anirudh Saraf, Elif Kutdemir Öncü
Items.Title: Quantifying model philosophy selection for instrument development
Items.Abstract: The selection of a model philosophy is a foundational decision in system development, directly shaping cost, schedule, technology maturation, and technical risk across the full lifecycle.    While the ECSS standards provide thorough guidance on the different types of system models, the process of selecting a specific model philosophy while quantitatively balancing programmatic constraints remains unique to each system and the organization responsible for its development, and continues to be a challenging task amid evolving programmatic and technical constraints.    This paper presents a mathematical trade-off methodology for comparing competing model philosophies for a representative scientific instrument. Two alternative model philosophies are evaluated: one emphasizing early risk reduction through additional physical models, and another prioritizing reduced cost and accelerated schedule at the expense of higher technology risk.

Items.Authors: Giovanni Boato, Davide Greggio, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Mohamed Bournane, Demetrio Margin, Silvio Di Rosa, Roberto Ragazzoni, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Marco Dima, Jacopo Farinato, Matteo Aliverti, Andrea Baruffolo, Luigi Lessio, Alessandro Ballone, Federico Battiani, Maria Bergomi, Elena Carolo, Simonetta Chinellato, Stefano Ciroi, Simone Di Filippo, Tania Sofia Gomes Machado, Luca Marafatto, Matteo Munari, Kalyan Kumar Radhakrishnan Santhakumari, Enrico Cappellaro, Paolo D'Avanzo, Marco Riva, Piero Giubilato, Mario Salatti, Paolo Spanò, Valentina Viotto, Simone Zaggia
Items.Title: MezzoCielo: a new concept telescope capable of fisheye fov at seeing limited resolution
Items.Abstract: MezzoCielo (Italian for “half of the sky”) is a new telescope concept that delivers a fisheye field of view at seeing-limited resolution. The design centres on a 1.8 m monocentric collector: a glass sphere filled with a low refractive index liquid. The hemispherical focal plane is tiled with ~1 000 identical correctors, each covering a 2.5° patch of sky, giving an instantaneous footprint of roughly 10 000 square degrees. The metre-class entrance pupil, multiplied by the hundreds of correctors, provides a total collecting area equivalent to that of a 30-m-class telescope. We review the current status of the instrument and present the optical design, along with performance analyses. We characterise the refractive fluid’s optical properties and quantify the image-quality degradation caused by its strong temperature dependence, then outline mitigation strategies. We also report on throughput estimates and sketch the roadmap for future development.

Items.Authors: Massimo Robberto, Stephen A. Smee, Robert H. Barkhouser, Stephen C. Hope, John J. Piotrowski, Dana Koeppe, Mario Gennaro, Zoran Ninkov, Megan E. Donahue, Andrei Tokovinin, Randolph P. Hammond, Al Harding
Items.Title: Operational capabilities and performance of SAMOS at the end of Science Commissioning Phase
Items.Abstract: We present the operations and performance of the SOAR Adaptive-Module Optical Spectrograph (SAMOS) at the end of its science commissioning phase. SAMOS is a digital-micromirror-device (DMD) based multi-slit spectrograph and imager deployed at the SOAR ground-layer AO system SAM. SAMOS relays the full AO-corrected 3′×3′ field of view onto the central 1Kx1K section of a large-format DMD. Each DMD mirror projects a 0.18”x0.18” field to either a spectroscopic or parallel imaging channel. The DMD is thus used to generate a slit-mask pattern with near-instantaneous setup time. The spectrograph spectral range is covered by two low resolution gratings over the full 4,000-10,000A visible range at R ∼ 2500. High resolution spectroscopy, R~10,000, is provided over two limited spectral ranges, 4,500-5,150A in the blue, and 6,0000-7,000A in the red, for a 0.33′′ slit width. A fifth grating is being procured that will offer R~10,000 in the "Gaia RVS" Calcium-triplet 8,500-8,750A region.

Items.Authors: Florian Kanal, Ralf Jedamzik, Ina Mitra, Clemens Kunisch, Martin Kurz, Antoine Carré, Janina Krieg
Items.Title: Progress on a new ZERODUR® composition for picometer-stability requirements in astronomy
Items.Abstract: For astronomical telescopes, ZERODUR® is the low-thermal-expansion material of choice due to its thermal properties and its processability. Regardless that since its introduction ZERODUR® is used in many high-precision scientific studies and high-tech industries for decades, SCHOTT is constantly working on material-property improvements. A recent adaptation of the ZERODUR® composition showed significant advancements in both thermal as well as mechanical properties. Here we report on further progress on the material characterization with special respect to future requirements in ultra-precision astronomical programs. In addition, we show first steps for qualifying the material for upcoming space missions and astronomical projects.

Items.Authors: Donghwan Hyun, Donggeun Tak, Gregory Paek, Myungshin Im, Ji Hoon Kim, Seo-won Chang, Hyeonho Choi, Won-hyeong Lee, Danhyeuk Seol, Jangho Bae
Items.Title: Py7DT: data reduction pipeline of the 7-Dimensional Telescope
Items.Abstract: We present Py7DT, a comprehensive Python package for processing data from the 7-Dimensional Telescope (7DT), a medium-band telescope array located in Chile. With its 20 telescopes and 40 filters, 7DT performs both rapid follow-ups of targets of opportunity (ToO) and three-tier surveys of the southern sky. The pipeline uses a parallelized processing framework that can leverage both CPU and GPU resources and prioritize urgent ToO tasks. The code is modular and portable, serving as a standard tool for end users to reprocess 7DT data with custom configurations, supporting the  diverse scientific goals of 7DT – from pixel-based analysis of galaxies to exoplanet transits – while remaining flexible and easy to maintain. The pipeline also features multi-level logging, automatically generated quality-assurance statistics and flags, and web-based real-time status monitoring to reduce the workload on the small operations team.

Items.Authors: Arika Egan, Laura Mayorga, Erin May
Items.Title: The multi-telescope hot Jupiter survey: updated instrument design & performance
Items.Abstract: Exoplanet atmospheric dynamics are best probed with spectroscopic phase curves, which measure how a planet’s flux changes with longitude and orbital position to reveal heat transport. Linked properties—temperature, pressure, winds, composition, and stellar irradiation—shape clouds, hazes, and the hottest and coldest regions. Hot Jupiters, with periods under ~10 days, provide ideal laboratories for atmospheric studies, but current missions cannot obtain full phase curves for planets with periods >5 days. The Multi Telescope Hot Jupiter Survey (MiTHOS), a SMEX-class concept, will address this gap using a constellation of small satellites carrying identical spectrometers spanning 0.5–5 μm. MiTHOS will gather phase curves for over 80 hot Jupiters and use shared calibration stars to remove instrument-specific systematics. Here, we present updated optical designs and throughput estimates demonstrating MiTHOS’s ability to resolve key questions in atmospheric dynamics.

Items.Authors: Alondra Solá, Clement Hottier, Myriam Rodrigues, Cyril Pannetier, Jay Stephan, Tim Morris, Polly Gill, Muhammad Shaheer Niazi, Sven Toucheboeuf, Gauri Padalkar, Roser Pello, Mathieu Puech, Gavin Dalton, Alessandro Meoli, Christian Surace, Marrie Larrieu, María Luisa García-Vargas, Thomas Augusteijn, Kacem El Hadi, Ruben Sanchez-Janssen, Fatima De Frondat
Items.Title: Twinpicks: a graph-based performance simulation tool for the design phase of complex instruments
Items.Abstract: Twinpicks is a graph-based performance simulation tool developed for MOSAIC@ELT, permitting continuous monitoring and verification of key performance indicators during the evolution of the instrument design. This allows for early risk identification and a rapid design/verification loop by quantifying the impact of design choices on the performance metrics.

Items.Authors: Javier G. Del Hoyo, Luis Rodriguez de Marcos, Joshua Hancock, Andrew Howe, Mateo Batkis, Joshua Vawdrey, Manuel Quijada, Richard Vanfleet, David Allred
Items.Title: Near perfect efficiency far-ultraviolet multilayer dielectric reflectors for astrophysics spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Spectral band-selecting far-ultraviolet (FUV) filters are pivotal optical components in spectrograph instruments allowing for isolated spectral line observations essential in the study of the warm-hot phase of the circumgalactic medium, electronic transitions and the structures of molecules, and the physical and analytical chemistries of the intergalactic medium. FUV Bragg reflectors have been demonstrated as viable band-selecting components in spectrographs exhibiting high spectral efficiency >95%, however, environmental instability of the components results in redshift of the peak efficiencies, structural coating failure due to high stresses, and reduced efficiency at the short end of the FUV spectrum. We present FUV Bragg reflectors produced utilizing reactive physical vapor deposition (rPVD) methods and novel lithium-based fluoride compounds. We demonstrate environmentally stable Bragg reflectors reaching peak FUV efficiencies of >99% at Lyman alpha (121.6 nm) and C IV (154.9 nm).

Items.Authors: Hiromichi T. Fujii, Shingo Matsumura, Naoki Sakaguchi, Haruyasu Ohno, Kotaro Ona, Shin Utsunomiya, Naoki Isobe, Aoi Takahashi, Iona Kondo, Hirokazu Kataza, Fumihiko Usui
Items.Title: Custom-engineered super Invar: Exceptional dimensional stability and magnetic properties for space applications
Items.Abstract: Next-generation space observatories in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) demand unprecedented dimensional stability. We present IC-LTX, a custom-engineered Super Invar alloy developed to overcome conventional limitations: cryogenic phase instability, geomagnetic magnetostriction, and long-term secular drift. By optimizing the composition to 33 mass% Ni and 3 mass% Co, it suppresses martensitic transformation below -100°C while achieving a coefficient of thermal expansion below a few x 10^-7 /K near 0°C. Under LEO geomagnetic fields, IC-LTX exhibits a zero-strain plateau, keeping magnetostrictive strain below 10^-8. Furthermore, restricting carbon to 0.011 mass% and implementing an accelerated pre-aging treatment at 315°C confirmed a secular growth rate below 0.1 ppm/year during a 5-year study. By achieving this thermal, magnetic, and temporal "trinity of stability," IC-LTX establishes a new standard for precision space structures, including missions such as JASMINE.

Items.Authors: Shao-zhen Zhu, Hao-ran Ma, Yu Ning, Wen-qing Qu, Xin Luo, Baolong Chen, Hong-fei Zhang, Jian Wang
Items.Title: Design of a performance test system for MCT infrared detectors
Items.Abstract: The Mercury Cadmium Telluride (MCT) detector is a cornerstone device for astronomical observations in the short-wave infrared (SWIR) band. The ongoing development towards large-format, multi-channel MCT detectors places stringent demands on test systems concerning noise, consistency, and readout speed. To address this, we have designed and implemented a dedicated high-speed, low-noise drive and readout system. This system is built around an FPGA core capable of generating customizable timing sequences, integrated with low-noise multi-channel bias supply modules and high-speed, high-precision readout paths. This architecture effectively ensures a low-noise test environment and high signal fidelity. It was demonstrated that the system's intrinsic channel-to-channel variation is significantly smaller than the inherent inter-channel differences of the MCT detector under test, guaranteeing the accuracy of characterization.

Items.Authors: Gaia Gaspar, Marcin Sawicki, Nelson Nunes, Rubén J. Díaz, James E. H. Turner
Items.Title: Feasibility of up-the-ramp sampling under variable sky for ground-based spectrographs
Items.Abstract: Many modern near-infrared instruments employ HAWAII-2RG (H2RG) detectors with integration times that can reach 300-600s. Up-the-ramp (UTR) sampling offers advantages over Fowler sampling, including superior cosmic ray rejection and noise reduction, but requires fitting linear ramps from 30-60 reads. Ground-based K-band sky brightness has been reported to vary by 3-10\% on timescales of minutes, potentially introducing systematic errors and compromising photometric accuracy. Additionally, UTR data formats involve higher-dimensional FITS files with larger file sizes impacting observatory operations.     We present a feasibility study using the GIRMOS Data Simulator with high-fidelity flux budgets and empirical K-band sky variations estimated, for Mauna Kea, from Gemini-NIRI at 10-20s cadence. Using a Monte Carlo approach we assess whether linear ramp fitting remains viable under variable sky conditions, quantify SNRs and systematic biases, and report nightly data volume estimates.

Items.Authors: Naif AlMalik, Gianluca Lombardi, Noorihan Deraz
Items.Title: The AlUla Manara Observatory Complex: an integrated concept for an advanced Multi-Aperture Scientific Platform and Visitor Centre
Items.Abstract: The AlUla Manara Observatory Complex is a new facility under development in AlUla, north-western Saudi Arabia, led by the Royal Commission for AlUla. Centered on an advanced research platform hosting a 4m-class and two 2m-class telescopes, and complemented by a unique public-engagement centre, the complex is designed to provide national access to modern observational astronomy, scientific training, and international collaboration. Its shared infrastructure supports both research and outreach through unified maintenance, technical services, and safety systems, alongside controlled access, low-impact circulation, and dark-sky-compliant lighting to preserve site integrity. The scientific platform is being developed around three telescopes, with the 4m aperture defined by comprehensive site assessment and designed for optical-IR astronomy with future AO capability, while the two 2m-class systems enable time-domain studies, and training to strengthen long-term national research capacity.

Items.Authors: Antonin H. Bouchez, Michael Bottom, Sylvain Cetre, Mahawa Cissé, Richard Dekany, Percy Gomez, Charlotte Guthery, Philip Hinz, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Marc Kassis, Scott Lilley, Jessica R. Lu, Jim Lyke, Eduardo Marin, Dimitri Mawet, Maïssa Salama, Max Service, Andrew J. Skemer, Avinash Surendran, Jacob Taylor, Marcos van Dam, Maria Vincent, Ed Wetherell, Peter Wizinowich
Items.Title: The Keck Observatory adaptive optics program
Items.Abstract: We report on current and future upgrades to the twin 10 m W. M. Keck Observatory adaptive optics capabilities. The KAPA laser tomography upgrade to Keck I will provide improved image quality and sky coverage for faint-object science. The HAKA/IWA upgrade to Keck II adds a 2844-actuator deformable mirror and an infrared pyramid wavefront sensor to dramatically improve contrast around bright guide stars. This system will feed the SCALES coronagraphic integral field spectrometer and the HISPEC fiber-fed spectrometer. The future Keck I AO Facility will further extend these capabilities with a new laser projection system and an adaptive secondary mirror. In parallel with these science-driven upgrades, the Keck Observatory is pursuing technology development projects focused on segmented mirror sensing and control for space telescopes and the testing of new wavefront sensors, coronagraphs, and photonic devices.

Items.Authors: Fabiola Norambuena, Justo Gonzalez, Jonathan Antognini, Vicente Coopman, Matias Gonzalez, Camila Martinez
Items.Title: An Off-Sky Calibration and Data-Model Validation Framework for ALMA in the Wide Sensitivity Upgrade Era
Items.Abstract: The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) is undergoing a major transformation through the Wide Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU), including an evolution of the ALMA Science Data Model (ASDM). Key calibration tasks are being migrated from real-time operations to an asynchronous, offline domain, reducing operational risk and enabling scalable, robust workflows. We present an Off-sky Processing Framework that reprocesses archived observations to generate WSU-format ASDMs and subsequently trigger QA0 pipelines. Its automated end-to-end pipeline enables large-scale regression testing of software releases, providing continuous developer feedback while ensuring reproducibility, traceability, and consistent validation of both data-model and calibration changes, all without impacting operations. This approach exemplifies Data Lifecycle Engineering principles and supports reproducible, cost-effective calibration and validation practices for modern radio observatories.

Items.Authors: Bart Vandenbussche, Sibo Van Gool, Leonardo Peri, Camille Pirat, Gert Raskin, Pierre Royer, Maddalena Reggiani, Hugues Sana, Julien Storm, Louis Storm, Dirk Vandepitte, Mathijs Arts, Tjorven Delabie, Wim De Munter, Jacob Pember, Bram Vandoren, Jorg Versluys, Nectarios Chari, Thomas Borel, Dominic Bowman
Items.Title: Building the CubeSpec mission: in-orbit demonstration of high-resolution spectroscopy on a 12U CubeSat
Items.Abstract: CubeSpec is an in-orbit demonstration CubeSat mission in the ESA technology programme, developed and funded in Belgium. The programme is now in phase C/D. Environmental qualification is finalising and building, testing and verification of the spacecraft and payload flight model has started. The project is on track for launch readiness end 2026. We present the final design of the mission and the results of test of engineering, qualification and flight models.  CubeSpec will measure high-resolution time series of spectral line profiles in massive stars to probe their internal structure. This requires a spectral resolution R > 50,000 (~0.01 nm) and SNR ≥ 200.   CubeSpec features several technological innovations: a 3-axis fine steering mirror bringing arcsecond level line-of-sight stability, a compact optical payload with fully ceramic 10x20cm cassegrain telescope, a cross-dispersed echelle spectrograph, compact FPGA CMOS sensor readout and a deployabe sun shade.

Items.Authors: Arno P. Schoenmakers
Items.Title: The overpromise trap: How cognitive biases distort projects - and what to do about it
Items.Abstract: Many innovation and technology development projects are based on over-promised outcomes which leads to stakeholder disappointment and budget overruns. Causes for delays and issues are often cited in the technical or resource availability domain. However, human cognitive biases play an important, but not always visible or realized, role in this. By better understanding and recognizing human cognitive biases and their impact on the project life-cycle, a project manager can lower their impact on project outcome. I present a set of important biases and their effects on projects, based on our own experiences at ASTRON.

Items.Authors: Luke C. Johnson, Dirk Schmidt, Andrew Beard, Scott Gregory, Lukas Rimmele, Thomas Rimmele, Erik Starman, Friedrich Woeger
Items.Title: Construction status of the DKIST Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics upgrade
Items.Abstract: The upgrade of the National Science Foundation's 4-meter Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) from a classical single-conjugate adaptive optics system to a multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) system is currently underway. Eventually, three deformable mirrors (DM) and nine wavefront sensors (WFS) will expand the corrected field of view to up to 1 arcmin in MCAO mode and to 2 arcmin in ground layer AO (GLAO) mode. In deployment phase 1, planned for late 2026, we will install the MCAO wavefront sensor, which will enable DKIST to use GLAO. Two high-altitude deformable mirrors, conjugate to 4km and 11km, will be installed in phases 2 and 3. The DM4km is a 1600-actuator DM manufactured by Xinetics and is nearing completion. We present the design, construction and laboratory testing of the MCAO wavefront sensor unit which features a novel mechanism to adjust the location of the WFS guide regions. We also report on factory acceptance testing of the DM4km and new plans for the DM11km.

Items.Authors: Danilo Gonçalves, Vanessa Macanhan, Angelo de Souza, Márcio Vital de Arruda, Railson Falcão, Getulio C. Vasconcelos, Andersan Paula, Bruno V. Castilho
Items.Title: Development of NiTi Alloys by Selective Laser Melting from Elemental Ni and HDH Ti Powders
Items.Abstract: NiTi shape memory alloys were produced by selective laser melting (SLM) using blended elemental oxyreduction Ni and HDH Ti powders as a low-cost alternative to pre-alloyed feedstocks. The study investigated the effect of a laser-remelting strategy on the consolidation of in-situ alloyed NiTi. Powder morphology, elemental distribution, and apparent porosity were evaluated by SEM, EDS, and digital image analysis. The remelting approach significantly reduced porosity and improved densification compared with conventional single-pass processing, demonstrating its potential for enhancing the fabrication of NiTi alloys from elemental powders.

Items.Authors: Sebastian J. Diebold, Jürgen Barnstedt, Jörg Bayer, Lauro Conti, Hans Rudolf Elsener, Christoph Kalkuhl, Daniel M. Schaadt, Darleen J. Rau, Thomas Schanz, Beate Stelzer, Klaus Werner
Items.Title: Microchannel plate detector development for ultraviolet astronomy
Items.Abstract: Observational data from the UV wavelength range is crucial to solve a number of astrophysical puzzles. Consequently, there is a number of upcoming UV missions from cubesats up to the future flagship Habitable Worlds Observatory. Besides novel instrument concepts and improved coatings, advanced detectors are key for the success of these missions. The microchannel plate (MCP) detector technology offers a unique asset in the UV: the combination of single-photon counting and visible-blindness.    The UV hardware group at IAAT develops a versatile MCP detector system that addresses the complete UV band. While a sealed-tube design is limited to wavelengths above 118 nm, an open-face variant covers also the whole far- and extreme-UV. Both use the same readout: a coplanar cross-strip anode and FPGA-based electronics.    In this contribution we report on the status of the detector development, present the latest characterization results, and give an outlook on the mission prospects.

Items.Authors: Sophia A. Sánchez-Maes
Items.Title: Event-based solar imaging in the H-α wing at the Dunn Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: We present the first demonstration of event-based solar imaging in the H-alpha wing at the Dunn Solar Telescope. A commercial event-sensing camera and a traditional frame-based imager observed the same small solar subfield simultaneously under adaptive-optics-corrected conditions. The event camera observed the H-alpha wing (known to exhibit fast chromospheric dynamics, including signatures associated with reconnection) using a universal birefringent filter. The resulting dataset includes active regions and flare-related activity. We describe the observational setup, the calibration and alignment steps used to prepare the data, and initial comparisons between the asynchronous event stream and the conventional images. These results provide the first on-sky evaluation of event-based sensing for resolving rapid solar fine structure in a ground-based environment.

Items.Authors: Chang Jin Oh, Andrew E. Lowman, Jamison Noenickx, In-Ung Song, Christian Baker, Robert Besuner, Patrick Jelinsky, Michael E. Levi, Timothy N. Miller, Claire Poppett, Connie Rockosi, David J. Schlegel
Items.Title: Large segmented aperture widefield telescope for Stage 5 Spectroscopic Experiment (SPEC-S5)
Items.Abstract: The Stage-5 Spectroscopic Experiment (Spec-S5) is a next-generation, all-sky spectroscopic facility designed to address fundamental questions in cosmology and astrophysics following the legacy of DESI. The SPEC-S5 telescope optical requirements set the primary mirror aperture to 6 m diameter and the field to 2.17 degrees circular, over a spectral band of 360 – 980 nm. To avoid the cost of constructing a new observatory, the baseline approach is to modify an existing 4 meter telescope structure to support the larger primary.   This paper presents the optical and mechanical design and analysis of the primary mirror and secondary mirror supports, optical tube structure, wavefront sensing and control, and system level error budget.

Items.Authors: Shaojie Chen, Sarik Jeram, Emma Jiayi Xu, Xuefeng Yao, Mark Barnet, Ting Li, Suresh Sivanandam, Zain Azam, Ziang Chen, Sarah He, Aditya Khandelwal, Chris Cheng, Daksh Singh, Coby Silayan, Laly Boyer
Items.Title: Prototyping the next-generation spectrograph for space exploration: DMD-Based Multi-Object Spectrograph Design and Production
Items.Abstract: Digital Micromirror Devices (DMD) are compact, programmable, and commercially available devices that can be leveraged in multi-object spectrograph (MOS) designs for both ground- and space-based instruments. Our team is developing a DMD-based MOS spectrograph (DMD-MOS) for a Planewave 0.5m telescope, which serves as the pathfinder of next-generation spectrographs for space exploration. DMD-MOS is composed of imaging and spectrograph channels and can obtain hundreds of object spectra simultaneously. The complete system, including the core optical system, software, calibration subsystem, and telescope interface, was commissioned in early June 2026. This DMD-MOS prototype successfully achieved first light and obtained stellar spectra of Vega, and further testing is planned. The measured spectra reproduced the expected stellar absorption features and demonstrated successful end-to-end operation of the complete observing chain, reinforcing the viability of DMD-based MOS spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Ágnes Mika, Arno Schoenmakers, Ilse van Bemmel, Pieter Benthem
Items.Title: Introducing the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle for improving the execution of instrumentation projects
Items.Abstract: For several years now, ASTRON has been actively engaged in improving its project execution with the aim of enhancing the quality and timely delivery of major radio astronomy facilities. The latest improvements focus on introducing the “Check” and “Act” facets of the “Plan-Do-Check-Act" cycle. This includes project reviews, up-to-date financial dashboards, clear responsibility and escalation lines, the application of project categories based on risk levels and budget size, and the tailoring of project management and systems engineering according to them.

Items.Authors: Rain Naylor, Nicole Melso, David Schiminovich, Matthew Werneken, Meghna Sitaram, Ruimian Zheng, Nidhi Shah
Items.Title: LIONESS science payload design: taming nanosatellite packaging constraints for future science missions
Items.Abstract: The Line Imaging Orbiter for Nanosatellite-Enabled Spectrographic Surveys (LIONESS) is a 6U CubeSat carrying a microlens-based narrowband integral field spectrograph payload. LIONESS stands to greatly improve our understanding of the circumgalactic medium (CGM), conducting high signal-to-noise observations by leveraging the low sky background in orbit. LIONESS observes the prominent Hα emission line, dispersing narrowband spectra. It aims to locate the missing baryons surrounding galaxies and map the gas kinematics in the CGM. The LIONESS spectrograph utilizes a retro-reflective Offner relay design, with the convex mirror replaced with a convex grating operating near-Littrow. A crucial benefit of this design is its small footprint, keeping the optical components within the packaging of a nanosatellite, and decreasing reflective surfaces that could lose crucial photons. We will discuss this design, the incorporation of new technologies, and its application to future space missions.

Items.Authors: Michael Langmayr, Yashvi Sharma, James Don Neill, Elijah Anakalea-Buckley, Prakriti Gupta, Max Brodheim
Items.Title: Modern Orchestration for Astronomical Data Reduction
Items.Abstract: Modern astronomical data reduction pipelines must handle growing data volumes, complex instrument configurations, and the need for reproducibility across varied computing environments. As part of developing the LRIS-2 pipeline for the W. M. Keck Observatory, we present a new architecture that applies mature data-engineering practices, particularly workflow orchestration using Prefect, to create a more transparent, modular, and resilient system. The pipeline represents each step as an observable task in a directed acyclic graph, enabling selective re-execution, real-time state visibility, and parallel processing. A dual-layer primitive model supports both clear, portable Python implementations and optional compiled C primitives that accelerate critical operations without changing scientific results. Designed for compatibility with the Astropy ecosystem, this approach promotes sustainability, community adoption, and a scalable template that other instruments and observatories can adapt.

Items.Authors: Tayyaba Zafar, Simon Ellis, Dani Guzman, Anilkumar Mailvaganam, Benjamin Courtney-Barrer, Heike Ebendorff-Heidepriem, Tamal Mukherjee, Imam U. Aalia, Arihant Raidani, Samuel Carlson, Bahareh S. Salmasi, Xuanyi Lyu, Srivardini Ayyappan, Hubert A. Moser, Ka Wu, Andrija Djordjevic, Mustafa Al Arat, Agnieszka Botor-Probierz, Kai Baessler, Yunle Wei, Yosuke Minowa, Jose Luis Carrillo Martinez
Items.Title: ZBLAN fibres for wide-field infrared astronomy
Items.Abstract: ZBLAN fibres offer exceptionally low loss and broad transparency into the mid‑infrared, making them promising for next-generation wide-field infrared astronomy. This paper focuses on the practical challenges of preparing ZBLAN fibres for telescope integration, including transmission characterisation, polishing techniques, connectorisation, and bend‑radius constraints. We review the material properties that enable performance gains in the 0.9–4.5 µm range and compare ZBLAN ZrF4 with alternative fluoride families such as InF3. Recent fabrication advances, including microgravity‑drawn fibres, are discussed in the context of reducing devitrification and scattering. This work establishes a foundation for deploying ZBLAN fibres in AO-assisted infrared instrumentation and highlights their potential to unlock new science in high-redshift galaxy studies.

Items.Authors: J. Kolb
Items.Title: From infancy to facility: AO systems deployment at ESO observatories
Items.Abstract: The 14 adaptive optics systems offered by ESO for Science Operation at our facilities in Chile (and as many decommissioned) form the largest AO deployment in any observatory. ESO's AO journey started at the historical site of La Silla and will continue in the near future with the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) at Cerro Armazones.  Those different systems have been and will be put in operation by various Consortia of institutes, in close collaboration with ESO in order to efficiently feed their client instruments and seamlessly integrate in the Observatory's operation scheme.  We present aspects of designs and challenges for systems installed on site, with precursors and prototypes like COME-ON and MAD, instrument-integrated systems like NAOS, SINFONI-AO or SAXO, or facility-designed systems like the AOF and GRAVITY+ AO. We emphasize standardized key components (RTCs, DMs, LGS, algorithms) as well as automation and robustness of operation, and draw a perspective for the coming projects.

Items.Authors: Fabien Grisé, Nicholas Kruczek, Mélissa Alliguié, Kevin France, David Le Mignant, Randall McEntaffer, Jean-Claude Bouret, Kjetil Dohlen
Items.Title: UV echelle grating development for the Pollux instrument
Items.Abstract: Pollux is a UV spectrograph and spectropolarimeter under consideration for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The instrument architecture includes three cross-dispersed, high resolution spectrograph channels (R>75,000–100,000) to cover its far-UV, mid-UV, and near-UV spectral range (101-472 nm).  We present our prototyping efforts for the mid-UV echelle grating including efficiency measurements and modeling results. Building on these results, we describe our approach to fabricate and characterize an improved Si-etched grating optimized for HWO's science requirements. While current prototype gratings demonstrate the fundamental feasibility of our fabrication approach and meet Pollux's MUV channel minimum efficiency requirements, continued improvements in lithography and wet etching processes will enhance overall performance while maintaining low scatter. These developments address key technology gaps as enabling technologies for future UV spectroscopy missions at all scales.

Items.Authors: Xiangqun Cui, Dehua Yang, Hua Bai, Haikun Wen, Fanghua Jiang, Shouwei Hu, Tingting Liu, Dongsheng Niu, Ding-qiang Su, Ya-nan Wang
Items.Title: Conceptual design of a 50m telescope with large-aperture and wide-field for optical and infrared surveys
Items.Abstract: We present a conceptual design for a novel next-generation 50-m aperture telescope, the Spherical Wide-field Extremely Large Telescope (SWELT), optimized for both wide-field spectroscopic surveys and high-precision photometric observations in the optical and infrared bands. To achieve the very large aperture with a large field of view (FOV), a spherical primary mirror and with a set of array correctors positioned before the primary focus. The primary mirror is segmented to balance fabrication complexity, cost, and active correction performance. An innovative solution to the telescope mounting structure beyond the conventional alt-azimuth designs is considered to get a highly stiff structure with minimal mass, ensuring dynamic stability and low operational costs for the massive 50-m aperture. The design highlights the balance between large aperture, wide-field capability, and cost-effective construction, paving pathway towards next-generation ground-based optical/infrared telescopes.

Items.Authors: Shelley A. Wright, Aaron Brown, Shree Doshi, Benjamin Godfrey, Jerome Maire, Dan Werthimer, Jamie Holder, Nikolas Korzoun, Carolyn Heffner, Andrew Howard, Paul Horowitz, Alyssa Johnson, Wei Liu, Sophie Nathanson, Yuriy Popovych, Elisa Pueschel, Nicolas Rault-Wang, Sruthiranjani Ravikularaman
Items.Title: Panoramic SETI: science objectives and experimental setup
Items.Abstract: The Panoramic Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (PANOSETI) observatory is a multi-purpose experiment designed to explore fast optical phenomena—from nanoseconds to seconds—across wide fields of view. Over the past five years, PANOSETI has advanced through extensive R&D to optimize its telescopes, detector readout electronics, and data analysis software for remote, autonomous operation. Its science program spans optical technosignature (SETI) searches, ultra-high-energy (UHE) gamma-ray investigations, and time-domain astrophysics targeting rare, fast transients. PANOSETI also enables multi-messenger synergies with neutrino and gravitational-wave observatories, as well as solar system and near-Earth transient studies. The distributed array provides coincidence detection and all-sky monitoring of UHE Cherenkov events. We will present an overview of the major science cases, along with a technical update on the program and its future directions.

Items.Authors: Tony B. Hull, Esther del Pino Rosendo, Janina Krieg, Thomas Westerhoff, Ralf Jedamzik, Florian Gollier
Items.Title: Crucial material factors that underlie stability of spaceborne mirrors
Items.Abstract: Material-imposed dimensional stability is more complex than consideration of the lowest Coefficient of Thermal Expansion (CTE) or the highest Thermal Diffusivity (TD). In material selection for an environment, it is crucial to recognize the presence of gradients T(xyz) and that CTE is not a scalar but depends on the temperature of operation. Thus, the thermal distortion at point xyz is defined by the product T(xyz)*CTE(T). Furthermore, when comparing materials of similar CTE, its homogeneity CTE(xyzT) is also crucial. We will consider the instability response of a hypothetical 1.5-meter diameter mirror, under the gradient resulting from being heated from the back to maintain a surface temperature in the range 270K to 300K. The materials, CTE Tailored ZERODUR® and SiC will be compared with results evaluated as should be done when selecting mirrors for stable space telescopes.

Items.Authors: Kostas Valeckas, Arthur M. Kadela, Joonas K. M. Viuho, Lise B. Christensen, Johan P. U. Fynbo, Jacob Clasen, Michael I. Andersen, Anton Norup Sørensen, Bo Milvang-Jensen, Kasper E. Heintz
Items.Title: Introducing the data-reduction pipeline for the Nordic Optical Telescope Transient Explorer spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The NOT Transient Explorer (NTE) is a new instrument for the Nordic Optical Telescope (NOT) that will provide both imaging and spectroscopic capabilities. In spectroscopic mode, NTE covers the wavelength range from 3200 Å to 2.2 μm in a single exposure through three independent arms. Designed to support rapid-response transient science, NTE requires observing tools that operate under strict time-critical constraints, including fast and reliable data reduction. In this talk, we present the current status of the NTE spectrograph data-reduction pipeline, including first results using simulated data. Our approach adapts the widely used and well-documented PypeIt package (Prochaska et al. 2020, JOSS) into a fully automated, rapid, and centralized data-reduction workflow. We also introduce new capabilities developed specifically for NTE that are not available in native PypeIt, such as echelle order stitching across the full spectral range.

Items.Authors: Marcos Reyes García-Talavera, Sergio Fernández, Icíar Montilla Garcia, José Miguel Delgado, Eduardo González, Roberto López, Manuel Luis Aznar, Roberto Simoes, José Marco de La Rosa, Ana Núñez, Jesús Patrón-Recio, Marta Puga, Josefina Rosich, Víctor Sánchez-Béjar, Óscar Tubío, Gianluca Lombardi, Héctor de Paz, Manuel Huertas, Daniel Gómez, Ismael Álvarez, Peter Wizinowich, Daniel Reverte, Enrique Joven, Josep Miret
Items.Title: On-sky performance and results of the Gran Telescopio Canarias Adaptive Optics system with the infrared camera Grancain
Items.Abstract: GTCAO is the Adaptive Optics (AO) system of the 10-meter Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory (ORM). It includes a deformable mirror with 373 actuators and a Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensor with 312 subapertures, aiming for a 65% Strehl ratio in the K band under average atmospheric conditions with a bright natural guide star. GRANCAIN (GRAN CAmara INfrarroja) is the first scientific instrument for GTCAO, integrated in October 2025. This cryogenic camera, with a H2 detector, covers the J, H, and K bands and provides diffraction-limited images over a 22 × 22 arcsec field of view. It operates in seeing conditions up to 1.5 arcsec and at zenith distances up to 60°. The optical system features 2:1 magnification. Significant efforts were made to enhance the telescope's optical quality, including phasing the primary mirror for GTCAO. This paper presents results from Grancain's commissioning campaigns and improvements for diffraction-limited imaging.

Items.Authors: Oleg Djazovski, Denis Laurin, Stephane Roberge, Jason Rowe, Kelsey Hoffman, Stanimir Metchev, Frederic Grandmont, Anne-Sophie Poulin-Girard, Marie-Eve Ducharme, Olivier Daigle
Items.Title: Optical telescope assembly and detector systems for compact astronomy satellites
Items.Abstract: This paper presents the advancement of the miniaturized optical telescope assembly (OTA) for exoplanetary astronomy and development of an ultra-sensitive detector system compatible with small satellite constraints. The test results have shown that the OTA achieves low PSF variations across wavelength and temperature ranges over a wide field enabling precision photometric observations of exoplanet transits candidates. The imaging performance and sensitivity of a compact detector compare favorably to that of ground-based Electron Multiplying CCD (EMCCD) and Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) imaging systems.

Items.Authors: Patrick Caillier, Florian Kerber, Sébastien Egner, Eric Emsellem, Markus Schöller
Items.Title: The project triangle in support of ESO instrumentation projects
Items.Abstract: Scientific instruments in combination with cutting-edge telescope produce the data for doing science by ESO’s user community. For their development ESO forms a core project office consisting of a project manager, a project engineer and a project scientist. This project triangle is completed by expert staff from the relevant engineering disciplines provided through a matrix-based organisation forming the ESO instrument project follow-up team working closely with the instrument consortium.  The authors of this paper replicate this project triangle at the line management level being the heads and deputies of the instrument science, systems engineering and project management departments. We meet on a regular basis to discuss and address relevant developments. We’ll share ESO’s experience with this project triangle and how the structured combination of engineering, science and management exploits the natural tension between the roles and deliver added value to the instrument projects.

Items.Authors: April D. Jewell, Nathan Bush, John Hennessy, Michael Hoenk, Todd Jones, Shouleh Nikzad, Charles Shapiro
Items.Title: Advanced ultraviolet silicon detector technologies enabling CubeSat, SmallSat, Explorer-class, and Flagship missions
Items.Abstract: Advances in instrument technologies are enabling exciting new science in astrophysics, planetary science, and heliophysics. JPL’s delta doping technology yields ultrastability and record sensitivity in silicon-based detectors, which has enabled smaller spacecraft— including sounding rockets, suborbital balloons, and CubeSats—to perform sensitive science measurements previously only possible with larger satellite platforms. Here we discuss recent deployments and developments of JPL’s UV detector and coatings technologies, including on the recently launched astrophysics Star-Planet Activity Research Activity CubeSat (SPARCS), technology advancement with the Heterodyne OH Lunar Miniaturized Spectrometer (HOLMS) prototype, and the status of detector development for the astrophysics Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission. These advancements are critical to demonstrating readiness for future missions, including, the Habitable Worlds Observatory mission concept in development.

Items.Authors: Jean-François Sauvage, Pierre-Louis Mayeur, Cyril Petit, Nicolas Védrenne, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: PROVIDENCE : a ground station for space observation
Items.Abstract: PROVIDENCE will be an ambitious optical research platform primarily dedicated to the observation of. It is a 2.5m adaptive telescope optimized for High Angular Resolution. Installed at the Observatoire de Haute Provence, the project targets dual applications, covering satellite and debris observation, astronomical observation, innovative instrumentation and cross-disciplinary issues around environmental and atmospheric characterization, laser focusing and optical telecoms (QKD and deep space communications). In this presentation, we give technical details on this station, flowing down from its science objectives to the technical specifications and functionalities. PROVIDENCE will embed high-level tracking capacities, will propose 2 Nasmyth and 4 Coudé foci allowing operational and research instrumentation. Currently at the study and prototyping stage, the station will be ready for the observation of the near-Earth asteroid APOPHIS in April 2029.

Items.Authors: Sam Ragland, Guido Brusa, Alessandro Cavallaro, Daniel Caywood, Laird Close, Juan Carlos Guerra, Michael Lefebvre, Douglas Miller, Mark Smithwright, Gregory Taylor, Christian Veillet, Xianyu Zhang, Roberto Biasi, Marlène de Sepibus, Daniele Gallieni, Jared Males, Elena Masciadri, Brandon Mechtley, Fernando Pedichini, Camilo Weinberger, Heejoo Choi, Guido Agapito, Matthieu Bec, Maria Bergomi, Al Conrad, Steve Ertel, Simone Esposito, Jamison Noenickx, David Munoz, Chang Jin Oh, Eliad Peretz, Enrico Pinna, Roberto Ragazzoni, Fabio Rossi, Joseph Shields
Items.Title: The path to agile extreme adaptive optics at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory
Items.Abstract: We highlight recent exciting AO science and discuss ongoing efforts to elevate the AO systems to facility-class status, along with strategies to transform them into Agile Extreme Adaptive Optics (AgXAO) systems to operate effectively under harsh and variable seeing conditions.  We share lessons learned from recent service missions, including the critical effort to recover from water intrusion in one of the ASMs, where the magnet side of the thin shell was recoated. Additionally, we present the status of refurbishing the Magellan ASM to serve as a compatible spare for the LBT, including upgrades to the Magellan reference body, along with long-term mitigation plans to replace the entire ASM or its electronics with next-generation hardware. We present LBTO’s AO operations and technological advancements in the context of Extremely Large Telescopes, highlighting its role as a testbed for advanced wavefront control algorithms, astrophotonics experiments, and machine learning applications.

Items.Authors: Paul Hirst
Items.Title: Automatic DRAGONS data reduction within the Gemini Observatory Archive
Items.Abstract: The Gemini Observatory Archive stores and distributes both raw and reduced data to Gemini users. While all raw data is automatically transferred in near-real-time to the archive, until recently only limited numbers of reduced data sets have been uploaded by the observatory and visitor instrument teams. However, we have recently implemented infrastructure to automatically reduce data from several observing modes of the facility instruments on both Gemini telescopes within the archive system, vastly increasing the quantity of reduced data available. Incorporating the Gemini DRAGONS data reduction software into GOA enables the automatic reduction of science and calibration data within the archive system, as well as the monitoring of site characteristics, system performance, instrument health, and data quality. The large number of observing modes and instrument configurations present a significant challenge in automatic data processing, compared for example to survey-style observing.
